claims.text: FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles have a size-dependent thermal response.
Smaller FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles undergo structural changes at lower temperatures than larger FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles.
The relevant structural changes may include surface segregation or phase transformation.
As-synthesized FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles are uniform, single-phase solid solutions, likely with an FCC structure.
Pulsed laser deposition on a SiN membrane can be used to prepare the proposed FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles.
In situ aberration-corrected STEM heating can be used to investigate the atomic-scale thermal response of high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles.
Molecular dynamics simulations can complement in situ STEM measurements of nanoparticle thermal behavior.
Sub-10-nm high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles can be synthesized directly on a SiN heating membrane for in situ TEM.
A temperature interval from approximately 298 to 973 K is usable for in situ STEM investigation of high-entropy-alloy nanoparticle thermal behavior.
Heating enhances atomic mobility and can produce pronounced diffusion in quinary high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles.
Atomic diffusion and surface effects become more pronounced as FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticle size decreases.
The higher surface-to-volume ratio of smaller nanoparticles causes segregation, phase transformation, or surface-layer melting to begin earlier.
Heating can cause formation and melting of a compositionally segregated surface layer in a quinary nanoalloy.
Smaller FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles will show surface-layer melting or phase evolution at lower temperatures than larger particles.
The size-dependent behavior is conditional on the vacuum and substrate conditions used during in situ STEM.
The response may differ under other environmental or processing conditions.
Exact transition temperatures, the detailed structural evolution, and quantitative temperature shifts with particle size are not established.
EDS mapping and electron diffraction can be used alongside STEM imaging to detect compositional segregation and phase evolution.
Absence of a systematic size-dependent shift in the onset temperature would falsify the proposed size-dependence.
